---
title: "Potential Outcomes and Identification"
---

The statistics of Part I lets us describe a joint distribution of covariates, treatments, and outcomes,
and from samples of that distribution it lets us estimate conditional expectations such as
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,X=x]$ and marginal expectations such as $\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (recall the conditional
expectation of @def-conditional-expectation and the estimators of Chapter 5). We can predict, classify,
and quantify uncertainty. What we cannot yet do is answer a counterfactual question: how would a
patient's outcome have changed had she received treatment $B$ instead of treatment $A$? The patient who
received $A$ supplies her outcome under $A$, which we observe; her outcome under $B$ is unobserved, and
it is unobservable in principle from this patient, because she did not in fact receive $B$ and cannot be
assigned to both treatments at once. This unobservability is the *fundamental problem of causal
inference*, and no amount of data from a single patient resolves it.

Every indirect treatment comparison, however elaborate, is ultimately a statement about such
counterfactuals: it claims that treatment $B$ would do better or worse than treatment $C$ in some target
population, even though no trial randomized those two treatments head to head. Before we can compare
treatments across studies, we must be able to say precisely what a treatment effect *is* and under what
conditions a population can recover it from data. That is the work of this chapter. We develop the
Neyman-Rubin potential-outcomes model (a bookkeeping device that gives every patient two outcomes, one
per treatment), which separates *what we want to know*, the counterfactual contrast, from *what we
observe*, the factual outcome under the received treatment. We state the stable-unit-treatment-value
assumption (the condition that makes "a patient's outcome under her own treatment" a well-defined object)
and the consistency identity (the algebra that links the observed outcome to the potential ones) that
bind the two together. We define the estimands an indirect comparison might target: the average treatment
effect, the effect on the treated, the effect on the controls, and the conditional average treatment
effect. We then isolate the two assumptions, ignorability (treatment is as good as random within
covariate strata) and positivity (every covariate stratum contains both treated and control patients),
that turn an unobservable counterfactual mean into an observable functional of the data, and we prove the
identification theorem for the average treatment effect by iterated expectation. Finally we prove that the
naive treatment-minus-control contrast equals the effect on the treated plus a selection-bias term, which
makes precise why adjustment is needed when treatment is not randomized.

Throughout we use the causal notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd): $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ are the potential
outcomes under control and active treatment, $T\in\{0,1\}$ is the treatment indicator, $X\in\mathcal{X}$
collects baseline covariates, $e(x)=P(T=1\mid X=x)$ is the propensity score, $\mu_t(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid
X=x]$ is the conditional mean potential outcome, $\tau(x)=\mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x)$ is the conditional average
treatment effect, and $\tau=\mathbb{E}[\tau(X)]$ is the average treatment effect. Two symbols we will lean
on heavily deserve to be named now, since they are not in the notation chapter: $P_X$ denotes the
*marginal distribution (law) of the covariates* $X$, and $\mathbb{E}_X[\,\cdot\,]$ denotes an expectation
taken *over that covariate distribution* (so $\mathbb{E}_X[h(X)]=\int h(x)\,dP_X(x)$). Both are spelled
out again where they first do real work. The development follows @hernan2020whatif and @rosenbaum1983, and
it corresponds to items B.1 through B.5 of the companion proof catalogue.

Two navigational notes before we begin. First, several results carry a bracketed
`[machine-checked: ...]` tag naming the corresponding lemma in the companion Coq development; those tags
are for readers auditing the formalization and can be safely skipped on a first reading. Second, the
probability facts we borrow from Part I (the tower property @thm-tower-property, dominated convergence
@thm-dominated-convergence, the graphoid axioms @thm-graphoid-axioms) are cited by number as we use them,
so you can follow the causal argument without re-deriving the underlying probability.

## A running clinical example {#sec-po-running}

We anchor the whole chapter in one small clinical picture and return to it at every turn. Imagine a
single center studying a **new drug** ($T=1$) against **standard care** ($T=0$) for a chronic disease.
The outcome $Y$ is a physical-function score at six months, on a scale where higher is better. Each
patient has a *baseline prognostic status* $X$, coarsened to two levels: $X=1$ for favorable baseline,
$X=0$ for poor baseline.

Consider two patients. *Alice* has favorable baseline ($X=1$). If she takes the new drug she would score
$Y(1)=24$; if she takes standard care she would score $Y(0)=20$. Her personal benefit from the new drug
is $24-20=4$ points. *Bob* has poor baseline ($X=0$), with $Y(1)=14$ and $Y(0)=10$, again a benefit of
$4$ points. The catch is structural: Alice can be given only one treatment, so we ever see only one of her
two numbers. If she takes the new drug we record $24$ and her $20$ stays hidden forever; if she takes
standard care we record $20$ and her $24$ is the counterfactual we can never observe. The same holds for
Bob and for every patient.

These two patients are representatives of the two covariate strata of the fully worked population in
@exm-confounding-gformula, whose stratum means are exactly Alice's and Bob's numbers. We will use Alice
and Bob to make each definition concrete, and near the end we will put real probabilities on this
population and watch a naive analysis report a benefit of $9$ when the truth is $4$. Keep the picture in
mind: two hidden numbers per patient, one revealed, and a chapter's worth of machinery devoted to
recovering *averages* of the hidden ones.

## The Neyman-Rubin model {#sec-po-rubin}

The framework begins by positing, for each unit, not one outcome but two: the outcome that would be
realized under each of the two treatments. These are the potential outcomes. They live on the same
probability space as the observed data, and they are ordinary random variables; what distinguishes them
is that only one of the two is ever revealed for any given unit.

Before the formal definition, fix the picture the formalism encodes. Think of $\omega$ as *one patient*,
and of the probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ as the mathematical version of the sentence "draw a
patient at random from the population." The set $\Omega$ is the population of patients; $P$ says how likely
each kind of patient is to be drawn; a random variable is any number attached to a patient (her covariates,
her treatment, her outcome). In this language Alice and Bob are two particular points $\omega\in\Omega$,
and a potential outcome is just a rule that assigns each patient the score she *would* get under a given
treatment.

::: {#def-potential-outcome}
## Potential outcomes
Fix a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ whose points $\omega\in\Omega$ index the units of a
population. A pair of **potential outcomes** is a pair of random variables
$$
Y(0):\Omega\to\mathbb{R},\qquad Y(1):\Omega\to\mathbb{R},
$$
where $Y(1)(\omega)$ is the outcome unit $\omega$ would experience under active treatment and
$Y(0)(\omega)$ the outcome it would experience under control. More generally, for a treatment label
$t\in\{0,1\}$ we write $Y(t)$ for the potential outcome under treatment $t$, so that $Y(t)=t\,Y(1)+(1-t)\,Y(0)$
as a function of the label. Both $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ are assumed to be well-defined, measurable, and (unless
stated otherwise) integrable, that is, $Y(0),Y(1)\in L^1(P)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Record potential_outcomes`, `Definition potential_outcome`]

**Reader translation.** Every patient carries two numbers, the outcome she would get under the new drug
and the outcome she would get under standard care. For Alice these are $Y(1)(\omega)=24$ and
$Y(0)(\omega)=20$. Only the one matching the treatment she actually receives is ever seen; the other is
hidden but no less real. A note on the two kinds of "$t$": a *lowercase* $t\in\{0,1\}$ is a fixed label
we choose (as in "the potential outcome $Y(t)$ under treatment $t$"), whereas the *uppercase* $T$ we meet
next is the random treatment a patient actually receives. Watching this lowercase-versus-uppercase
distinction (notation convention 2 of [Notation](/notation.qmd)) saves a great deal of confusion; the
switch is doing real work every time it appears.

The causal effect of treatment on a *single* unit is the difference between that unit's two potential
outcomes. We name it because it is the quantity an idealized experiment on one patient, repeated in two
parallel worlds, would measure.

::: {#def-individual-effect}
## Individual treatment effect
The **individual treatment effect** (ITE) for unit $\omega$ is
$$
\tau(\omega)=Y(1)(\omega)-Y(0)(\omega).
$$
It is itself a random variable on $\Omega$, measurable whenever $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ are. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** The ITE is one patient's personal benefit or harm from treatment, the difference
between her two hidden numbers. Alice's ITE is $24-20=4$ and Bob's is $14-10=4$. It is the thing we would
most like to report to a patient, and, by the very next theorem, exactly the thing no data set can ever
deliver.

The individual effect is exactly what we would like to know and exactly what we can never observe. The
reason is structural, not a matter of sample size: for each unit, one of the two potential outcomes is
realized and the other is *counterfactual*, the outcome under the treatment the unit did not receive. The
next theorem makes this precise. In plain words it says: *two different worlds can produce identical
observed data yet have different causal effects, so no analysis of the observed data alone can recover the
effect.* Formally, two genuinely different populations, differing in their individual effects and even in
their average effect, can produce identical observed data, so no procedure that reads only the observed
data can recover the individual effect.

::: {#thm-fundamental-problem}
## The fundamental problem of causal inference
Let the **observed outcome** under a treatment assignment $T:\Omega\to\{0,1\}$ be
$Y=Y(T)$, that is, $Y(\omega)=Y(T(\omega))(\omega)$. There exist two pairs of potential outcomes
$(Y(0),Y(1))$ and $(Y'(0),Y'(1))$ on a common space, and a common assignment $T$, such that the observed
data $(T,Y)$ and $(T,Y')$ have the same joint distribution, yet the individual treatment effects differ
at some unit:
$$
Y(1)-Y(0)\;\not\equiv\;Y'(1)-Y'(0).
$$
Consequently no function of the observed data $(T,Y)$ alone equals the individual treatment effect, and
no such function equals the average individual effect either.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Lemma ITE_unobservable`]

::: {.proof}
We exhibit two worlds that agree on everything observable and disagree on the effect. Take any nonempty
$\Omega$ and let every unit be treated, $T(\omega)=1$ for all $\omega$. Define
$$
\text{World A:}\quad Y(1)\equiv 1,\ Y(0)\equiv 0,
\qquad
\text{World B:}\quad Y'(1)\equiv 1,\ Y'(0)\equiv 1 .
$$
Because $T\equiv 1$, in both worlds the observed outcome is the potential outcome under treatment:
$Y=Y(1)\equiv 1$ in World A and $Y'=Y'(1)\equiv 1$ in World B. Hence $(T,Y)$ and $(T,Y')$ are both the
constant pair $(1,1)$ and have identical joint laws. The individual effects, however, are
$Y(1)-Y(0)\equiv 1$ in World A and $Y'(1)-Y'(0)\equiv 0$ in World B, which differ at every unit; the
average effects $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]=1$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y'(1)-Y'(0)]=0$ differ as well.

Now suppose some measurable functional $\Psi$ of the observed data satisfied $\Psi(T,Y)=Y(1)-Y(0)$ in
every world. Applied to the two worlds above, $\Psi$ receives the *same* argument $(1,1)$ in both, so it
returns the same value; but the targets $Y(1)-Y(0)$ and $Y'(1)-Y'(0)$ differ. This contradiction shows no
such $\Psi$ exists. The identical argument with the constant targets replaced by their expectations rules
out a functional returning the average effect. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This impossibility is the logical warrant for the entire book. Because *no* method,
however clever, can recover an individual effect from observed data, every estimand we pursue afterward, in
regression, in network meta-analysis, and in indirect treatment comparison alike, is a *population
average* rather than a person-level prediction. When a later chapter targets an average effect and not a
personalized one, this theorem is the reason. The rest of the present chapter is the disciplined response
to it: recover averages when individual effects are hopeless.

The construction in the proof is deliberately extreme: with everyone treated there are no controls, so the
control outcome $Y(0)$ is pure counterfactual and the data carry no information about it. The remainder of
the chapter is the disciplined response to this problem. We cannot recover individual effects, but with
the right structural assumptions we can recover *averages*. The first such assumption concerns how the
observed outcome is generated from the potential ones.

## SUTVA and the consistency identity {#sec-po-sutva}

Writing $Y=Y(T)$ already smuggles in an assumption. It presumes that the outcome a unit displays under its
received treatment is its own potential outcome under that treatment, unaffected by which treatments other
units received and unambiguous as to which "version" of the treatment was given. These are the two
components of the stable-unit-treatment-value assumption. Before the formal statement: SUTVA is what lets
us pretend each patient lives in her own bubble, with one clearly defined "new drug" and one clearly
defined "standard care", so that her observed score is simply whichever of her two potential scores matches
the treatment she got.

::: {#def-sutva}
## Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)
Let the population receive an assignment vector $\mathbf{t}=(t_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}\in\{0,1\}^\Omega$,
and let $Y_\omega(\mathbf{t})$ denote the outcome unit $\omega$ would experience under the *full* vector
$\mathbf{t}$. The **stable unit treatment value assumption** consists of two parts.

- **(SUTVA-1) No interference.** Each unit's outcome depends on the assignment vector only through that
  unit's own component: for all $\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t}'$ and all $\omega$,
  $$
  t_\omega=t'_\omega\ \Longrightarrow\ Y_\omega(\mathbf{t})=Y_\omega(\mathbf{t}').
  $$
- **(SUTVA-2) No hidden versions.** There is a single, well-defined version of each treatment level, so
  that the label $t\in\{0,1\}$ determines the intervention unambiguously.

$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/CausalAssumptions.v`, `Definition SUTVA`, `Lemma no_interference_unit_level`]

**Reader translation.** SUTVA says two things in plain clinical terms. First, *no interference*: my outcome
depends on the treatment *I* take, not on who else in the study happened to be treated. Second, *no hidden
versions*: "the new drug" names one well-defined intervention, not a grab-bag of different doses or
regimens masquerading under one label. Only when both hold does it make sense to write a patient's observed
outcome as her own potential outcome under her own assignment, $Y=Y(T)$.

SUTVA is an assumption, not a theorem; it constrains the world, and it can fail. Interference fails in a
vaccine trial where one unit's vaccination lowers another unit's infection risk through reduced
transmission; hidden versions fail when "surgery" silently bundles several distinct procedures of
differing efficacy. The failure that most threatens indirect comparison is the second one across studies:
in a network of oncology trials, if one trial's "chemotherapy" arm delivers a higher dose than another's,
the single label "chemotherapy" hides two different interventions, SUTVA-2 fails, and the shared anchor on
which the indirect comparison depends is no longer one well-defined treatment. When you later read that two
trials must share a *common comparator*, this is the assumption being invoked. What SUTVA-1 buys,
mathematically, is the reduction from a vector-indexed family of outcomes to the two-potential-outcomes
setup of @def-potential-outcome: under no interference there is a function
$Y(\cdot)(\cdot):\{0,1\}\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ with $Y_\omega(\mathbf{t})=Y(t_\omega)(\omega)$ for every
assignment vector, because $Y_\omega(\mathbf{t})$ depends on $\mathbf{t}$ only through $t_\omega$. The
witness is $Y(t)(\omega):=Y_\omega(\mathbf{t})$ evaluated at any $\mathbf{t}$ with $t_\omega=t$, for
instance the constant vector $\mathbf{t}\equiv t$; no interference guarantees this does not depend on the
choice. We may therefore speak of $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ as unit-level random variables, exactly as the
catalogue records (corresponds to B.1 in the proof catalogue).

The bookkeeping is easiest to see in a table. Three patients, each with two potential scores, are assigned
a treatment; we observe the score in the assigned column and the other is counterfactual.

| Patient | Baseline $X$ | Assigned $T$ | $Y(0)$ | $Y(1)$ | Observed $Y=Y(T)$ | Hidden (counterfactual) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alice | $1$ (favorable) | $1$ (new drug) | $20$ | $24$ | $24$ | $Y(0)=20$ |
| Bob | $0$ (poor) | $0$ (standard care) | $10$ | $14$ | $10$ | $Y(1)=14$ |
| Carol | $1$ (favorable) | $0$ (standard care) | $20$ | $24$ | $20$ | $Y(1)=24$ |

Each row shows the fundamental problem in miniature: exactly one number per patient is observed and one is
forever hidden. The next result is simply the algebra of the "Observed $Y$" column.

With the two potential outcomes in hand and a treatment indicator $T$, the observed outcome is determined
by a case split: a treated unit shows its treated potential outcome, a control unit shows its control
potential outcome. The next result records this and its algebraic encoding, which is the workhorse of
every identification proof to come.

::: {#thm-consistency-identity}
## Consistency identity
Under SUTVA, with $T\in\{0,1\}$ the treatment indicator and $Y=Y(T)$ the observed outcome,
$$
Y = T\,Y(1) + (1-T)\,Y(0)
\qquad\text{pointwise on }\Omega.
$$ {#eq-consistency-identity}
Equivalently, $Y=Y(t)$ holds on the event $\{T=t\}$ for each $t\in\{0,1\}$. Moreover the treatment-masked
identities
$$
T\,Y = T\,Y(1),
\qquad
(1-T)\,Y = (1-T)\,Y(0)
$$ {#eq-consistency-masked}
hold pointwise.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Definition consistency`, `Lemma consistency_equiv`, `Lemma consistency_expectation`]

::: {.proof}
Fix $\omega$ and split on the value of $T(\omega)\in\{0,1\}$. If $T(\omega)=1$, the right-hand side of
@eq-consistency-identity is $1\cdot Y(1)(\omega)+0\cdot Y(0)(\omega)=Y(1)(\omega)$, which equals
$Y(\omega)=Y(T(\omega))(\omega)=Y(1)(\omega)$; SUTVA-1 makes $Y(1)(\omega)$ depend only on $\omega$'s own
assignment and SUTVA-2 makes it unambiguous, so this potential outcome is well-defined. If $T(\omega)=0$,
the right-hand side is $0\cdot Y(1)(\omega)+1\cdot Y(0)(\omega)=Y(0)(\omega)=Y(\omega)$. In both cases the
two sides agree, proving @eq-consistency-identity; the statement $Y=Y(t)$ on $\{T=t\}$ is the same case
split read one branch at a time.

For the masked identities, multiply @eq-consistency-identity by $T$ and use that $T$ takes values in
$\{0,1\}$, so $T^2=T$ and $T(1-T)=0$:
$$
T\,Y = T\bigl(T\,Y(1)+(1-T)\,Y(0)\bigr) = T^2\,Y(1) + T(1-T)\,Y(0) = T\,Y(1).
$$
Multiplying instead by $1-T$ and using $(1-T)^2=1-T$ and $(1-T)T=0$ gives $(1-T)Y=(1-T)Y(0)$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** The consistency identity is the single hinge that connects what we observe to what
we want. Every identification formula in this book, and every indirect-comparison estimator built on it,
passes through it: it is the one licensed move from an observed $Y$ to a potential outcome $Y(t)$.

The identity @eq-consistency-identity is, in the epidemiological literature, called *consistency*, a word
that unfortunately also names the convergence of an estimator; the two senses are unrelated and we keep
them apart by always saying "consistency identity" for the causal one. Its importance is that it lets us
trade the observed outcome for a potential outcome *inside conditional expectations*, on the event where
the corresponding treatment was received. This swap is the single bridge across which all identification
travels. The masked forms @eq-consistency-masked may look like a pointless multiplication by $T$, but the
point is to *isolate a single arm*: $TY=TY(1)$ keeps only the treated units and equates their observed
outcome with their treated potential outcome, discarding the controls. That is exactly the algebra behind
the inverse-probability-weighting estimator of the next chapter (@thm-ipw-unbiased), which reconstructs
$\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$ from the treated arm alone; the masked identity is what makes that arm-by-arm
reconstruction legitimate.

::: {#cor-consistency-swap}
## Outcome swap under consistency
Under SUTVA, for each $t\in\{0,1\}$ and any covariate $X$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,X] = \mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T=t,X]
\qquad\text{a.s. on }\{P(T=t\mid X)>0\}.
$$ {#eq-consistency-swap}
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Lemma consistency_treated_mean`, `Lemma consistency_control_mean`]

::: {.proof}
By @thm-consistency-identity, $Y=Y(t)$ everywhere on the event $\{T=t\}$. The claim is then an instance of
a general fact: a conditional expectation given $(T=t,X)$ depends on its integrand only through the
integrand's values on the event $\{T=t\}$. To see why, recall the defining property of conditional
expectation (@def-conditional-expectation and @eq-cond-exp-defining): $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\mid T=t,X]$ is
characterized by its integrals against test sets of the form $\{T=t\}\cap B$ with $B$ an $X$-measurable
set. For two integrands $f$ and $g$ that agree on $\{T=t\}$ we have $f\mathbf{1}_{\{T=t\}\cap B}=
g\mathbf{1}_{\{T=t\}\cap B}$ pointwise, so their defining integrals coincide for every such test set;
by the uniqueness clause of @def-conditional-expectation the two conditional expectations are therefore
a.s. equal. Applying this with $f=Y$ and $g=Y(t)$, which agree on $\{T=t\}$ by consistency, gives
@eq-consistency-swap wherever the conditioning event has positive probability. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** The corollary says: among patients with covariates $X$ who *actually received*
treatment $t$, their observed outcome and their potential outcome under $t$ have the same average. The
proviso is the honest limitation: this only speaks about patient types who are sometimes given treatment
$t$. It says nothing about the treated potential outcome of a patient type who is never treated, because
there is simply no one to average. The proviso $P(T=t\mid X)>0$ is exactly the positivity condition of
@sec-po-assumptions; without it the conditioning event $\{T=t,X=x\}$ can be null and the left-hand
conditional mean is not defined there.

## Estimands {#sec-po-estimands}

We cannot recover individual effects, so we target averages. Which average depends on the question. This
section names the standard estimands; the rest of the chapter is about identifying the first of them from
data. All are defined directly from the potential outcomes, with no reference yet to how treatment was
assigned, so they are properties of the population, not of any estimator.

One word carries a lot of weight here: *which* population. The "population" in each average is whichever
population the covariates $X$ are drawn from. In a randomized trial it is the enrolled sample; in a cohort
study it is the source population; in an indirect treatment comparison it is the decision maker's *target*
population, which may be neither trial's. An effect that is correct in one population can be wrong in
another, so keeping track of which population an estimand refers to is the single most important habit for
the rest of the book.

::: {#def-ate}
## Average treatment effect
The **average treatment effect** (ATE) is the population mean of the individual treatment effect,
$$
\tau := \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)].
$$ {#eq-ate}
It is the expected change in outcome if the entire population were switched from control to active
treatment. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Definition ATE`, `Lemma ATE_split`]

**Reader translation.** The ATE answers "if we treated *everyone* in this population instead of no one, how
would the average score change?" In the running example it will turn out to be $4$: the average patient
gains $4$ function points from the new drug.

The second equality in @eq-ate is linearity of expectation, the same step that the Coq lemma `ATE_split`
records; it already shows that the ATE is built from the two *marginal* mean potential outcomes
$\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$, each of which we will identify separately. Restricting the
average to the units who actually received treatment gives a different estimand, the one most relevant when
a regulator asks what a drug did for the patients who took it.

::: {#def-att}
## Average treatment effect on the treated
The **average treatment effect on the treated** (ATT) is
$$
\tau_{\mathrm{T}} := \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1],
$$ {#eq-att}
the mean individual effect among units with $T=1$. The symmetric **average treatment effect on the
controls** (ATC) is $\tau_{\mathrm{C}}:=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=0]$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Definition ATT`, `Definition ATC`]

**Reader translation.** The ATT restricts the question to the patients who *did* take the new drug: "for
those actually treated, how much did treatment help on average?" The ATC asks the mirror question of those
who received standard care. These differ from the ATE whenever the treated and untreated are different
kinds of patient, which is the usual situation outside a randomized trial.

::: {#def-cate}
## Conditional average treatment effect
For covariates $X$, the **conditional average treatment effect** (CATE) is the function
$$
\tau(x) := \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x] = \mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x),
\qquad \mu_t(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X=x],
$$ {#eq-cate}
the mean effect within the covariate stratum $X=x$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** The CATE is the effect *within a stratum of patients*: the average benefit among
favorable-baseline patients, and separately among poor-baseline patients. In the running example both
strata have CATE $4$, so the effect happens to be constant; in general it varies with $x$, and that
variation, called effect modification, is what makes an effect fail to carry from one population to another.
The CATE is therefore the building block of every cross-population argument later in the book.

The CATE refines the ATE by covariates, and the ATE is its average: by the tower property
(@thm-tower-property),
$$
\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]\,\bigr] = \mathbb{E}[\tau(X)],
$$ {#eq-ate-is-mean-cate}
which is the relation recorded in [Notation](/notation.qmd). This averaging is benign here because we are
on the identity (mean-difference) scale, where the average of a constant stratum effect is that constant.
*You do not need this yet, but a signpost for later:* on a nonlinear scale such as the odds ratio, a
constant stratum effect need not average to itself, a phenomenon called non-collapsibility. We flag it only
so the reader is not surprised in @def-non-collapsibility and @def-collapsibility, where it is developed
properly; on the identity scale of this chapter @eq-ate-is-mean-cate holds with no caveat.

It helps to see the four estimands side by side, together with where each surfaces in indirect comparison.

| Estimand | Symbol | Question it answers | Role in ITC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average treatment effect | $\tau$ | Effect if the whole target population switched control to treatment | The marginal, population-average target most population-adjustment methods aim at |
| Effect on the treated | $\tau_{\mathrm{T}}$ | Effect among patients who actually received treatment | The estimand when the question is specifically about the treated subgroup |
| Effect on the controls | $\tau_{\mathrm{C}}$ | Effect among patients who received control | The mirror image; appears in some transport arguments |
| Conditional effect | $\tau(x)$ | Effect within covariate stratum $X=x$ | The building block that carries effect modification across populations |

For orientation: the population-adjustment methods in this book (MAIC and STC in Part IV, ML-NMR in
Part V) are judged against an effect in a specified target population, on a stated effect scale, and the
usual target is a *marginal* (ATE-type) effect; Chapters 17 and 19 show when a method delivers a
conditional effect instead. The CATE is the object that makes such transport possible, because it is what changes
across populations when effect modifiers are distributed differently. The three population-level averages
are tied together by the proportion treated.

::: {#prp-ate-att-atc}
## Decomposition of the ATE over treatment groups
Let $p=P(T=1)$. Then
$$
\tau = p\,\tau_{\mathrm{T}} + (1-p)\,\tau_{\mathrm{C}}.
$$ {#eq-ate-decomp}
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Lemma ATE_decomposition`]

::: {.proof}
Apply the law of total expectation (@cor-total-expectation) to the integrable variable $Y(1)-Y(0)$, using
the partition $\{T=1\}\cup\{T=0\}$ of $\Omega$:
$$
\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]
= P(T=1)\,\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1] + P(T=0)\,\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=0],
$$
which is $p\,\tau_{\mathrm{T}}+(1-p)\,\tau_{\mathrm{C}}$ by @eq-att and the definition of $\tau_{\mathrm{C}}$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** The decomposition says the population effect is a weighted blend of the effect in the
treated and the effect in the controls. It holds with *no* assumptions whatsoever; in particular the ATE,
ATT, and ATC need not coincide. They coincide precisely when the individual effect is mean-independent of
treatment assignment, which is the situation a randomized experiment engineers and which the ignorability
assumption of the next section formalizes.

## Identifying assumptions: ignorability and positivity {#sec-po-assumptions}

The estimands of @sec-po-estimands are defined from potential outcomes, but data report only $(X,T,Y)$.
*Identification* is the act of writing an estimand as a functional of the observed-data distribution alone,
so that it could in principle be computed if we had infinitely much data. Two glosses are worth pinning
down, because a beginner can slip on both. A *functional* here means a map whose input is a whole
probability distribution and whose output is a number; identification asks whether the estimand is *pinned
down* by the distribution of the observable triple $(X,T,Y)$. This is a different question from
*estimation*, which asks how to compute a good approximation from a finite sample. Identification is the
infinite-data question; every estimator in later chapters presupposes that the answer to the identification
question is yes. Without further assumptions the ATE is *not* identified: @thm-fundamental-problem already
produced two populations with the same observed-data law and different ATEs. Two assumptions close the gap.
The first asserts that, within strata of the measured covariates, treatment is assigned as if at random,
independently of the potential outcomes. It comes in three strengths, and it is worth saying up front *why
there are three*: the identification proof below needs only the weakest (mean ignorability); randomization
delivers the strongest (strong ignorability) for free; and the balancing-score theory of the next chapter
needs the strongest. Keeping the three apart lets us assume exactly as much as each result requires.

::: {#def-ignorability}
## Ignorability (strong, weak, mean)
Let $X$ be baseline covariates. Three nested forms of **ignorability**, also called *no unmeasured
confounding* or *conditional exchangeability*, are:

- **Strong ignorability:** $\bigl(Y(0),Y(1)\bigr)\perp T \mid X$, the joint law of the two potential
  outcomes is conditionally independent of treatment given $X$.
- **Weak ignorability for $Y(t)$:** $Y(t)\perp T\mid X$ for the single label $t$ in question.
- **Mean ignorability for $Y(t)$:** $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]$ a.s.

Conditional independence is meant in the sense of @def-conditional-independence. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/CausalAssumptions.v`, `Definition strong_unconfoundedness`, `Definition weak_unconfoundedness`, `Lemma strong_implies_weak_unconf`]

**Reader translation.** In clinical words, ignorability says: *once we know a patient's covariates $X$,
knowing which treatment she was given tells us nothing about what her outcome would have been under either
treatment.* Within a stratum of $X$, the treated and untreated are exchangeable, as if a coin decided their
treatment. This is what randomization guarantees by design; in an observational study it is a hope, namely
that $X$ contains every characteristic that influenced both the treatment decision and the outcome. The
three forms differ in *how much* exchangeability they demand, summarized here:

| Form | Statement | Plain meaning | What it buys |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strong | $\bigl(Y(0),Y(1)\bigr)\perp T\mid X$ | Within a stratum, treatment is as-if-random with respect to *both* potential outcomes jointly | Identifies both arms; underwrites the balancing-score and propensity theory of Chapter 10 |
| Weak (for $Y(t)$) | $Y(t)\perp T\mid X$ | Same, but only for the single arm $t$ | Identifies the mean potential outcome $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)]$ for that one arm |
| Mean (for $Y(t)$) | $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]$ | Within a stratum, the *average* $Y(t)$ is the same among treated and untreated | The minimum needed to identify the ATE |

These three are genuinely different in strength, and the difference matters for which estimand can be
identified. The following lemma orders them.

::: {#lem-ignorability-hierarchy}
## Hierarchy of ignorability
Strong ignorability implies weak ignorability for both $t=0$ and $t=1$; weak ignorability for $Y(t)$
implies mean ignorability for $Y(t)$, provided $Y(t)\in L^1$.
:::

*Reader's note: the proof below is the most technical in the chapter. Its message is simply that the three
forms sit in a chain, strong $\Rightarrow$ weak $\Rightarrow$ mean. A reader meeting this material for the
first time may take the chain on faith and skip to the "What to remember" paragraph after it; the machinery
is here for completeness and for the Coq counterpart.*

::: {.proof}
*Strong implies weak.* By symmetry (graphoid axiom G1 of @thm-graphoid-axioms, which says
$A\perp B\mid Z\iff B\perp A\mid Z$) strong ignorability is $T\perp\bigl(Y(0),Y(1)\bigr)\mid X$. The
decomposition axiom (G2 of @thm-graphoid-axioms, which says that if $T$ is independent of a *pair* given
$X$ then it is independent of each *member* given $X$) states that $T\perp(U,W)\mid X$ implies
$T\perp U\mid X$; applying it with $U=Y(t)$ and $W=Y(1-t)$ yields $T\perp Y(t)\mid X$, that is, weak
ignorability for $Y(t)$, for each $t$.

*Weak implies mean.* Fix $t$ and write $V=Y(t)$. Conditional independence $V\perp T\mid X$ in the sense of
@eq-cond-indep is equivalent to $\mathbb{E}[f(V)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[f(V)\mid X]$ a.s. for every bounded
measurable $f$. We must extend this from bounded $f$ to the (possibly unbounded) identity function, and
this is where $V\in L^1$ enters. The idea is standard: approximate $V$ by bounded functions of $V$, apply
the identity for each, and pass to the limit. For $m\ge 1$ let $f_m(v)=\max(-m,\min(m,v))$ be the
truncation of $v$ to the interval $[-m,m]$; each $f_m$ is bounded and measurable, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[f_m(V)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[f_m(V)\mid X]\quad\text{a.s.}
$$
As $m\to\infty$ the truncation is undone: $f_m(V)\to V$ pointwise (once $m$ exceeds $|V(\omega)|$ the value
is untouched), and $|f_m(V)|\le|V|\in L^1$ provides a single integrable envelope for all $m$. By the
conditional form of dominated convergence (the conditional-expectation analogue of
@thm-dominated-convergence, obtained by applying that theorem inside each conditional expectation) the left
side converges a.s. to $\mathbb{E}[V\mid T,X]$ and the right side to $\mathbb{E}[V\mid X]$. Hence
$\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]$ a.s., which is mean ignorability. $\square$
:::

The converse implications fail: mean ignorability constrains only first moments and says nothing about the
rest of the conditional law, while weak ignorability for one label says nothing about the other. A concrete
illustration of the first gap: within a stratum $X=x$, suppose the treated potential outcome $Y(1)$ is
distributed as follows.

| Group | $Y(1)$ takes values | $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T,X=x]$ | $\mathrm{Var}(Y(1)\mid T,X=x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated ($T=1$) | $9$ or $11$, each with probability $\tfrac12$ | $10$ | $1$ |
| Untreated ($T=0$) | $5$ or $15$, each with probability $\tfrac12$ | $10$ | $25$ |

The two conditional means are both $10$, so *mean* ignorability for $Y(1)$ holds; but the two conditional
distributions differ (variances $1$ versus $25$), so $Y(1)\perp T\mid X$ *fails*. Mean ignorability is
strictly weaker, and, as the identification proof will show, strictly enough. (@exr-po-mean-vs-weak asks you
to turn this picture into a fully specified joint law and to check that the ATE is still identified.)

**What to remember.** The practical distillation of the hierarchy is this. A randomized trial aims to make
treatment independent of the potential outcomes, delivering *strong* ignorability for free. An
observational analysis must instead *condition on enough covariates* to make treated and untreated patients
comparable, and it can only hope for ignorability, never verify it. The ATE identification proof needs only
the weakest form, *mean* ignorability of each arm; we nonetheless usually *state* the strong form, for two
reasons. First, it is the natural output of randomization, so assuming it costs nothing there. Second, the
balancing-score and propensity-score theory of the next chapter genuinely needs the full joint
independence, not merely equal conditional means. So the extra strength is not wasted even though this one
theorem does not use it. Finally, ignorability is *untestable* from the observed data, because it constrains
the joint law of $T$ with the partly unobserved potential outcomes. A concrete example makes the danger
vivid: in rheumatoid arthritis or oncology, disease severity often drives both which treatment a clinician
chooses and how the patient fares. If severity is recorded, we can condition on it; if it is unmeasured, no
amount of modeling of the *recorded* covariates repairs the confounding, and no diagnostic run on the data
can reveal the omission. In a randomized trial ignorability holds by design, with $T$ assigned
independently of everything, including unmeasured characteristics; in an observational study it demands
that $X$ contain every confounder.

The second assumption guarantees that every covariate stratum actually contains both treated and control
units, so that the conditional means we will average are defined everywhere. The intuition is simple and
worth stating before the inequalities: *we cannot learn the treated outcome for a type of patient who is
never treated, nor the control outcome for a type who is never a control.* If, say, no frail patient ever
receives the new drug, the data contain no treated outcomes for frail patients, and the active-arm mean for
that stratum, hence the population ATE, cannot be recovered without extrapolation.

::: {#def-positivity}
## Positivity (overlap)
With propensity score $e(x)=P(T=1\mid X=x)$, **positivity** (or **overlap**) holds for treatment $t$ if
$$
P(T=t\mid X=x)>0 \qquad\text{for } P_X\text{-almost every } x\in\mathcal{X},
$$ {#eq-positivity}
where $P_X$ denotes the marginal distribution (law) of the covariates $X$, so that "$P_X$-almost every $x$"
means "for all $x$ except possibly a set of covariate values that occurs with probability zero."
Equivalently, weak positivity for both treatments is $0<e(x)<1$ a.s. **Strict positivity** strengthens
this to a uniform bound: there is $\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ with
$$
\varepsilon\le e(x)\le 1-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for } P_X\text{-almost every } x.
$$ {#eq-strict-positivity}
The reason for the stronger, uniform version is estimation stability: estimators that divide by $e(X)$ or
$1-e(X)$ (the weighting methods of the next chapter) have variance that blows up as the propensity nears
$0$ or $1$, so a bound bounded away from the endpoints is what keeps them well-behaved.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/CausalAssumptions.v`, `Definition weak_positivity`, `Definition strong_positivity`, `Lemma strong_implies_weak`]

**Reader translation.** Positivity says every kind of patient could, with some chance, have gone either
way: each covariate stratum contains both treated and control patients. Weak positivity asks only that the
chance be nonzero; strict positivity asks that it be *bounded away* from zero and one. In the
indirect-comparison setting this same condition reappears as *covariate overlap between studies*. Picture a
trial of drug $B$ that enrolled only elderly patients and a trial of drug $C$ that enrolled only young
patients: there is no covariate region where both drugs are represented, so no reweighting can turn one
trial's population into the other's, and the comparison of $B$ and $C$ rests entirely on extrapolation.

Strict positivity implies weak positivity: if $\varepsilon\le e(x)\le 1-\varepsilon$ with
$0<\varepsilon<\tfrac12$ then $0<\varepsilon\le e(x)$ and $e(x)\le 1-\varepsilon<1$, so $0<e(x)<1$. Weak
positivity is what identification needs, because @cor-consistency-swap and the iterated-expectation
argument require $P(T=t\mid X)>0$ almost everywhere; strict positivity is what *stable estimation* needs,
for the variance reason just given. That failure of overlap is the formal reason matching-adjusted indirect
comparison breaks down when trial populations barely overlap, taken up in Part IV, and it is the bridge to
the transportability conditions of @def-transportability. Together, ignorability and positivity are
@rosenbaum1983's **strong ignorability** (corresponds to B.3 and B.4 in the proof catalogue).

## Identification of the average treatment effect {#sec-po-identification}

We can now turn the unobservable ATE into an observable functional of the data. First, one piece of
notation that is the conceptual hinge of the entire argument. We have two "conditional mean outcome"
objects, and they look almost identical but mean very different things.

::: {#def-observed-regression}
## Observed outcome regression
The **observed outcome regression** is
$$
\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x) := \mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,X=x],
$$
the average *observed* outcome among units with covariates $x$ who *received* treatment $t$. It is to be
contrasted with the **potential mean** $\mu_t(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X=x]$ of @def-cate, the average
outcome those units *would* have under $t$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** $\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x)$ is a plain regression you can actually fit from data:
group patients by their covariates $x$ and their received treatment $t$, and average the outcomes you see.
$\mu_t(x)$ is the causal object we want but cannot see directly: the average outcome those patients *would*
have under $t$, treated and untreated alike. Identification is precisely the claim that, under ignorability
and positivity, these two coincide, $\mu_t(x)=\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x)$, so that a fittable regression equals
an unfittable counterfactual mean. Alongside it we use $\mathbb{E}_X[\,\cdot\,]$ for an expectation over the
covariate distribution $P_X$: in $\mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)\bigr]$ the *outer*
$\mathbb{E}_X$ averages the stratum-specific regression over the covariate distribution of the *target
population*, not over the treated group and not over the control group. This outer averaging is the exact
point where the choice of target population enters, and it is the bridge to population adjustment.

The engine of identification is a single chain of three equalities, applied to each potential-outcome
mean: peel off the covariate by the tower property, swap the treatment-assignment conditioning by
ignorability, swap the potential outcome for the observed one by consistency. We isolate the per-arm result
first.

::: {#lem-mean-potential-identification}
## Identification of a mean potential outcome
Assume SUTVA (so the consistency identity @eq-consistency-identity holds), mean ignorability for $Y(t)$,
and positivity for treatment $t$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y(t)] = \mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,X]\,\bigr].
$$ {#eq-gformula}
:::

::: {.proof}
We chain three identities; each equality is labeled by the fact that licenses it.

*Step 1 (tower property).* By @thm-tower-property, equivalently @cor-total-expectation, applied to
$Y(t)\in L^1$ and the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $X$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y(t)] = \mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]\,\bigr].
$$

*Step 2 (ignorability).* By mean ignorability for $Y(t)$, $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]$;
evaluating on the event $\{T=t\}$, which by positivity has positive probability for $P_X$-almost every $x$,
gives $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T=t,X]$ a.s., so
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y(t)] = \mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T=t,X]\,\bigr].
$$

*Step 3 (consistency).* By the outcome swap of @cor-consistency-swap,
$\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid T=t,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=t,X]$ on the positivity event, and substituting yields
@eq-gformula. Every conditional mean on the right-hand side is a functional of the observed-data law of
$(X,T,Y)$, so $\mathbb{E}[Y(t)]$ is identified. $\square$
:::

Subtracting the two arms gives the central identification theorem of the chapter, the result on which
standardization, inverse-probability weighting, and the entire machinery of Part IV ultimately rest.

::: {#thm-ate-identification}
## Identification of the ATE (adjustment formula)
Assume SUTVA, mean ignorability for both $t=0$ and $t=1$ (in particular, strong ignorability suffices),
and positivity for both treatments. Then the average treatment effect is identified by the **adjustment
formula** (also called the **g-formula** or **standardization formula**)
$$
\tau = \mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1,X] - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0,X]\,\bigr].
$$ {#eq-ate-identification}
In the notation of @def-observed-regression, this is
$\tau=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)-\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]$.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/CausalAssumptions.v`, `Theorem ATE_identification`]

::: {.proof}
Apply @lem-mean-potential-identification once with $t=1$ and once with $t=0$, which is legitimate because
the hypotheses hold for both labels, to obtain
$\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]$ and
$\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]$. By @def-ate and linearity of expectation
(@thm-tower-property gives the outer expectation, linearity gives the subtraction),
$$
\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]
=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]-\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]
=\mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)-\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)\bigr],
$$
which is @eq-ate-identification. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** The adjustment formula is the population target that every estimator in Part II and
every population-adjustment method later (G-computation, inverse-probability weighting, MAIC, STC, ML-NMR)
is built to estimate. Read it as a recipe: within each covariate stratum, take the difference of the
observed treated and control means; then average those stratum differences using the *target population's*
covariate distribution. When you later meet a "standardized" or "population-adjusted" indirect comparison,
this equation is what it is approximating. Because a numerical grip helps before the general theory settles,
we preview the running population immediately.

::: {#exm-gformula-preview}
## The adjustment formula at a glance
Take the two-stratum population of @exm-confounding-gformula (developed in full below): $X\in\{0,1\}$ with
$P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12$, observed regressions $\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(0)=10$, $\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(0)=14$,
$\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(1)=20$, $\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(1)=24$, and treatment three times more likely in the
favorable stratum. The adjustment formula @eq-ate-identification averages the *stratum* differences over
the *population* covariate split $\tfrac12,\tfrac12$:
$$
\tau=\tfrac12(14-10)+\tfrac12(24-20)=\tfrac12\cdot4+\tfrac12\cdot4=4 .
$$
The naive treatment-minus-control contrast, which instead averages over each arm's *own* (imbalanced)
covariate mix, will come out to $9$. The gap between $4$ and $9$ is the selection bias the next section
isolates; the full arithmetic, including the within-arm mixes, is in @exm-confounding-gformula.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The adjustment formula is the *population* statement; it tells an analyst with infinite data exactly how to
combine observable conditional means into the ATE. It also dictates the estimators of the next chapter, of
which two are central. *G-computation* models the inner regression $\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x)$ and averages
it over the empirical covariate distribution; it is identified by exactly this theorem and developed as
@thm-g-computation-unbiased. *Inverse-probability weighting* instead models the propensity score and
reweights, recovering the same target through @thm-ipw-unbiased, since the masked identity
@eq-consistency-masked gives $\mathbb{E}[TY/e(X)]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$, another route to
$\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)]$. You will meet these two first in the next chapter,
and afterward their combination, the doubly robust estimator @thm-aipw-double-robust, together with the
dimension-reducing balancing-score theory (@def-balancing-score, @thm-rosenbaum-rubin, @thm-ps-sufficiency)
that lets the scalar $e(X)$ stand in for the full covariate vector $X$. What the present theorem supplies is
the identification all of them implement.

::: {.remark}
It is worth dwelling on a subtlety the proof exposes. It used only *mean* ignorability for each arm, the
weakest form in @def-ignorability, together with positivity and SUTVA. Yet the assumption we usually
*state* is *strong* ignorability. Why assume more than we use? Two reasons, and they are not merely
stylistic. First, strong ignorability is the natural output of randomization: a trial that assigns
treatment by a coin flip makes $T$ independent of the entire joint law of $(Y(0),Y(1))$, not just of its
conditional means, so in a trial the strong form is available at no extra cost. Second, the balancing-score
and propensity-score theory of the next chapter genuinely requires the full conditional independence, not
equal conditional means alone; the result that conditioning on the scalar $e(X)$ can replace conditioning
on $X$ (@thm-rosenbaum-rubin) fails under mean ignorability. So the stronger assumption is doing real work
elsewhere in the book, even though this single identification theorem does not need it.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The naive contrast and selection bias {#sec-po-selection}

Why not simply compare the average outcome among the treated with the average among the controls? That
naive contrast is what an unadjusted analysis reports, and it is in general *not* the ATE. Here is the
picture before the algebra: in the running example, clinicians give the new drug preferentially to
favorable-baseline patients, so the treated arm is stacked with high scorers and the control arm with low
scorers. Even if the drug did nothing, the treated would out-score the controls simply because they were
healthier to begin with. That built-in head start is selection bias, and the next theorem locates it
exactly: the naive contrast equals the effect on the treated plus a term measuring how treated and control
groups would have differed even under no treatment.

::: {#thm-naive-selection-bias}
## The naive contrast equals ATT plus selection bias
Under SUTVA, define the **naive contrast**
$\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0]$. Then
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}
= \underbrace{\tau_{\mathrm{T}}}_{\text{ATT}}
+ \underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0]\bigr)}_{\text{selection bias}} .
$$ {#eq-naive-decomposition}
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`, `Lemma selection_bias_decomposition`]

::: {.proof}
By the consistency identity @thm-consistency-identity, $Y=Y(1)$ on $\{T=1\}$ and $Y=Y(0)$ on $\{T=0\}$, so
the observed group means are potential-outcome means:
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=1],
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0].
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0].
$$
Add and subtract the counterfactual control mean among the treated, $\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]$. We choose
precisely this quantity because it is the one bridge between the two observed means: it shares the
conditioning event $\{T=1\}$ with the first term (so the pair combines into an effect *among the treated*)
and it shares the potential outcome $Y(0)$ with the second term (so that pair compares the *same*
counterfactual across the two groups). Concretely,
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}
=\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]\bigr)
+\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0]\bigr).
$$
The first bracket is $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1]=\tau_{\mathrm{T}}$ by linearity of conditional
expectation and @eq-att; the second is the selection-bias term. This is @eq-naive-decomposition. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This decomposition is the precise reason an indirect comparison cannot simply pool
raw arm means across trials. The selection-bias term compares the *untreated* potential outcome $Y(0)$
between the group that took treatment and the group that did not; it is nonzero exactly when the two groups
would have differed even absent treatment, which is precisely confounding. It is an identity, not an
approximation: it holds under SUTVA alone, with no ignorability. Population adjustment exists to remove this
term. The next corollary shows it vanishes under the strongest form of ignorability, *marginal*
independence, which is what a randomized trial provides, and that this is what makes the naive contrast
valid there.

::: {#cor-naive-unbiased-rct}
## When the naive contrast is the ATE
Suppose SUTVA holds and treatment is *marginally* ignorable, $\bigl(Y(0),Y(1)\bigr)\perp T$ (no
conditioning on $X$), as in a marginally randomized experiment. Then the selection-bias term in
@eq-naive-decomposition is zero and
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tau_{\mathrm{T}}=\tau.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Marginal independence gives $\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]=\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]=\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0]$, so the
selection-bias term in @eq-naive-decomposition is $0$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tau_{\mathrm{T}}$.
Independence also gives $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]$, so $\tau_{\mathrm{T}}=\tau$.
$\square$
:::

Here "marginally randomized experiment" means the simplest randomized design: treatment is decided by one
coin flip for every patient, the *same* flip probability for all, with no conditioning on covariates. This
is the plain randomized controlled trial a health researcher already knows; the word "marginally" only
signals that the coin ignores $X$ entirely, which is why the independence in the corollary holds without
any conditioning. (A *stratified* trial, which flips a differently biased coin within each stratum of $X$,
delivers only the *conditional* independence of @def-ignorability, and there one must still adjust.) When
ignorability holds only *conditionally* on $X$, as in an observational study or in two trials with
different case mixes, the selection-bias term is generally nonzero and the naive contrast is biased; the
remedy is to condition on $X$ and average, which is exactly the adjustment formula @eq-ate-identification.
This is the formal reason indirect comparisons cannot simply pool raw arm means across studies, and it
motivates every population-adjustment method in Parts IV and V.

## A worked example: confounding, the g-formula, and selection bias {#sec-po-example}

We now put concrete numbers to the whole machinery in a single population, verifying the adjustment formula
and the selection-bias decomposition by hand. This is the population Alice and Bob live in: the two
covariate strata are their favorable ($X=1$) and poor ($X=0$) baselines, and the stratum means are exactly
their potential scores. The example is deliberately built on the identity scale with a *constant*
conditional effect, so that the only thing separating the naive contrast from the ATE is confounding, not
the non-collapsibility studied in @exm-noncollapsible-or; that lets us see selection bias in isolation.

::: {#exm-confounding-gformula}
## Standardization undoes confounding in a two-stratum population
Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ be a binary prognostic covariate with $P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12$. Treatment is confounded
by $X$ through the propensity score
$$
e(0)=P(T=1\mid X=0)=0.25,\qquad e(1)=P(T=1\mid X=1)=0.75,
$$
so that the favorable-baseline stratum $X=1$ is three times as likely to be treated (clinicians steer the
new drug toward the patients who were already doing better). Assume SUTVA, strong ignorability, and
positivity (both $e$ values lie strictly in $(0,1)$). The conditional mean potential outcomes are
$$
\mu_0(0)=10,\quad \mu_1(0)=14,\qquad \mu_0(1)=20,\quad \mu_1(1)=24,
$$
so the conditional average treatment effect is constant, $\tau(0)=\tau(1)=4$. Under ignorability the
observable regressions equal these conditional means, $\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x)=\mu_t(x)$.

**True ATE by the adjustment formula (@eq-ate-identification).** Averaging the constant stratum effect,
$$
\tau=\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1(X)-\mu_0(X)] = \tfrac12(14-10)+\tfrac12(24-20) = \tfrac12\cdot 4+\tfrac12\cdot 4 = 4.
$$
Equivalently $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]=\tfrac12(14)+\tfrac12(24)=19$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]=\tfrac12(10)+\tfrac12(20)=15$,
giving $\tau=19-15=4$.

**The naive contrast.** Treatment selection skews the covariate mix within each arm. The joint cell
probabilities are $P(X=x,T=t)=P(X=x)\,e(x)^{t}(1-e(x))^{1-t}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&P(X{=}0,T{=}1)=\tfrac12(0.25)=0.125,\quad P(X{=}1,T{=}1)=\tfrac12(0.75)=0.375,\\
&P(X{=}0,T{=}0)=\tfrac12(0.75)=0.375,\quad P(X{=}1,T{=}0)=\tfrac12(0.25)=0.125.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence $P(T=1)=P(T=0)=0.5$, and the within-arm covariate distributions are
$$
P(X=1\mid T=1)=\frac{0.375}{0.5}=0.75,\qquad P(X=1\mid T=0)=\frac{0.125}{0.5}=0.25.
$$
The treated arm is covariate-shifted toward the favorable stratum, the control arm toward the
poor-baseline stratum. Using consistency, $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=1]$ and
$\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0]$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1]&=0.25(14)+0.75(24)=3.5+18=21.5,\\
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0]&=0.75(10)+0.25(20)=7.5+5=12.5,
\end{aligned}
$$
so the naive contrast is
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=21.5-12.5=9.0.
$$
The unadjusted analysis overstates the effect by more than a factor of two, reporting $9$ against the truth
of $4$.

**Selection-bias decomposition (@eq-naive-decomposition).** Because the conditional effect is the constant
$4$, the effect on the treated is $\tau_{\mathrm{T}}=\mathbb{E}[\tau(X)\mid T=1]=4$. The counterfactual
control mean among the treated and the factual control mean among the controls are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]&=0.25(10)+0.75(20)=2.5+15=17.5,\\
\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=0]&=0.75(10)+0.25(20)=7.5+5=12.5,
\end{aligned}
$$
so the selection bias is $17.5-12.5=5.0$. The decomposition checks out:
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tau_{\mathrm{T}}+\text{selection bias}=4+5=9.0 .
$$
The entire discrepancy between the naive contrast and the ATE is the $5.0$ of selection bias, created
because the treated would have had better untreated outcomes (mean $17.5$) than the controls did (mean
$12.5$), purely through the covariate imbalance the propensity score induces.

**Standardization recovers the truth.** The adjustment formula reweights the stratum-specific contrasts by
the *population* covariate distribution rather than the arm-specific one:
$$
\tau=\mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\mu_1^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)-\mu_0^{\mathrm{obs}}(X)\bigr]
=\tfrac12(14-10)+\tfrac12(24-20)=4 ,
$$
matching the true ATE and removing the bias entirely. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The example exhibits the chapter in miniature. The same observed data $(X,T,Y)$ produce a biased number
($9$) when contrasted naively and the correct number ($4$) when standardized, and the gap is exactly the
selection-bias term the decomposition isolates. Notice that ATE, ATT, and CATE all equal $4$ here, because
the effect is constant on the collapsible identity scale; had we measured the effect as an odds ratio the
marginal and conditional effects would have parted ways even with no confounding, which is the separate
phenomenon of @def-non-collapsibility and the subject of @def-collapsibility in Chapter 11. It is
worth separating two things this example might otherwise blur. The covariate $X$ here is a *prognostic
variable* (it predicts the outcome) that is *also a confounder* (it steers treatment), and that is why the
within-study effect is biased. In an indirect comparison the usual villain is different: it is an *effect
modifier*, a covariate that changes the size of the treatment effect across its levels, distributed
differently in two study populations. A baseline imbalance that involves only prognosis, with no effect
modification, biases the naive within-study contrast (as here) but need not obstruct the cross-study
transport of a *conditional* effect on a suitable scale. The distinction between prognostic variables,
confounders, and effect modifiers is the theme of Chapter 11 (@def-prognostic-variable,
@def-effect-modifier); keep it in view, because the whole logic of population adjustment turns on it.

## Why identification is the foundation of indirect comparison {#sec-po-bridge}

Everything so far concerned a *single* population. This closing section connects that single-population
identification to the multi-study problem the book exists to solve, in three steps: what carries over
within a study, what is needed to move across studies, and what therefore becomes central in later chapters.

**Within a study, identification is settled.** One population has one covariate law $P_X$, one propensity
score $e(x)$, one pair of observed regressions $\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}(x)$. The adjustment formula
@eq-ate-identification identifies the ATE in that population, and the selection-bias decomposition
@eq-naive-decomposition explains what goes wrong if we ignore the covariates. A randomized trial of $A$
versus $B$ identifies the $A$-versus-$B$ effect in the trial's own population; a trial of $A$ versus $C$
identifies the $A$-versus-$C$ effect in *its* own population. Nothing in this chapter compares $B$ with $C$.

**Across studies, indirect comparison is the same logic applied between populations.** To compare $B$ with
$C$ we exploit a shared anchor: the common treatment $A$. The structure is small enough to tabulate.

| Study | Arms | Within-study effect it identifies | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| $AB$ | $A$ vs $B$ | $d_{AB}$, the effect of $B$ vs $A$ in study $AB$'s population | supplies the $A$-vs-$B$ contrast |
| $AC$ | $A$ vs $C$ | $d_{AC}$, the effect of $C$ vs $A$ in study $AC$'s population | supplies the $A$-vs-$C$ contrast |
| target | $B$ vs $C$ | $d_{BC}=d_{AC}-d_{AB}$ (the effect of $C$ vs $B$), valid only if both refer to a *common* population | the quantity we actually want |

The subtraction $d_{BC}=d_{AC}-d_{AB}$ is the indirect (Bucher) comparison of Chapter 14. It is honest only
when the two within-study effects live in, or can be transported to, a *common* population; otherwise we are
subtracting effects defined in two different worlds. Transport across populations is governed by the very
two assumptions of this chapter, now read *between* studies rather than within one. Positivity becomes
covariate *overlap*: the studies' covariate ranges must intersect, or no reweighting can bridge them (the
elderly-only versus young-only picture of @sec-po-assumptions is exactly this failure). Ignorability becomes
the requirement that the covariates explaining between-study differences are *measured and adjusted for*,
formalized as the transportability conditions of @def-transportability and as the absence of the ecological
bias of @def-ecological-bias.

**What therefore becomes central later.** Three things that were benign or invisible in one population move
to the foreground across populations. First, the *estimand*: population-adjustment methods target a marginal
effect in a *stated target population*, so naming that population is now unavoidable. Second, *effect
modification*: a covariate whose distribution differs between studies and that modifies the effect will make
a within-study effect fail to transport, which is why the CATE, not just the ATE, is the object that must be
carried across. Third, the *effect scale*: benign here on the identity scale, it becomes decisive once
nonlinear links and the non-collapsibility of @def-collapsibility enter, because then even a correctly
transported conditional effect need not average to the marginal effect a decision maker wants. The next
chapter develops the estimators that implement the adjustment formula within a study; Chapters 11 and 12
extend identification to effect modification and transport; and Parts III to V build these into the
Bucher comparison, network meta-analysis, MAIC, STC, and ML-NMR that indirect comparison actually requires.

## Notes and references {#sec-po-notes}

The potential-outcomes model is due to Neyman, in the 1923 randomization analysis of agricultural
experiments (@neyman1923), and Rubin, who extended it to observational studies (@rubin1974); @holland1986
named the "fundamental problem of causal inference" used in @thm-fundamental-problem. Our treatment follows @hernan2020whatif throughout, with the
strong-ignorability formulation and the central role of the propensity score from @rosenbaum1983. The
adjustment formula @eq-ate-identification is the simplest instance of Robins's g-formula (@robins1986); the
letter "g" stands for *generalized*, since the same construction generalizes to sequences of treatments
given over time, where it becomes the g-computation algorithm. This chapter corresponds to items B.1
through B.5 of the companion proof catalogue: potential outcomes and SUTVA (B.1, @def-potential-outcome,
@def-sutva), the consistency identity (B.2, @thm-consistency-identity), ignorability in its three forms
(B.3, @def-ignorability), positivity (B.4, @def-positivity), and the identification of the ATE (B.5,
@thm-ate-identification). The estimators that the adjustment formula underwrites, namely
inverse-probability weighting, G-computation, and the doubly robust augmented estimator, are catalogue items
B.6 through B.12 and are developed in the next chapter as @thm-ipw-unbiased, @thm-g-computation-unbiased,
@thm-aipw-double-robust, and @thm-eif-bound, together with the balancing-score and propensity-score theory
@def-balancing-score, @thm-rosenbaum-rubin, and @thm-ps-sufficiency.

Several results carry machine-checked tags pointing to the companion Coq development; a reader auditing the
formalization can follow them via Appendix G, and every other reader may ignore them. The fundamental
problem is `ITE_unobservable` in `theories/PotentialOutcomes.v`; the consistency identity and its masked and
swapped forms are `Definition consistency`, `Lemma consistency_equiv`, `Lemma consistency_expectation`,
`Lemma consistency_treated_mean`, and `Lemma consistency_control_mean` in the same file; the estimands and
their decomposition are `Definition ATE`, `Definition ATT`, `Definition ATC`, `Lemma ATE_split`, and
`Lemma ATE_decomposition`; and the selection-bias decomposition is `Lemma selection_bias_decomposition`.
The assumptions and the ATE identification live in `theories/CausalAssumptions.v`: SUTVA and the
no-interference reduction are `Definition SUTVA` and `Lemma no_interference_unit_level`; ignorability is
`Definition weak_unconfoundedness` and `Definition strong_unconfoundedness` with the ordering
`Lemma strong_implies_weak_unconf`; positivity is `Definition weak_positivity` and
`Definition strong_positivity` with `Lemma strong_implies_weak`; and the identification theorem is
`Theorem ATE_identification`. The Coq development states the probabilistic content (the tower property, the
locality of conditional expectation, and the conditional-independence consequences) as named hypotheses on
abstract expectation operators, exactly as the pen-and-paper proofs here invoke @thm-tower-property,
@cor-total-expectation, @thm-graphoid-axioms, and @def-conditional-independence from Chapter 4; the proofs
in this chapter supply the measure-theoretic justifications the Coq statements take as inputs.

The worked example @exm-confounding-gformula is original to this text.

## Exercises {#sec-po-exercises}

A starred exercise ($\star$) has a full worked solution in Appendix F; the unstarred ones are for practice.
The first two are gentle warm-ups; the later ones build to short proofs.

::: {#exr-po-warmup-ite}
## Warm-up: reading potential outcomes
**(Warm-up.)** Recall Alice from @sec-po-running: her potential function scores are $Y(1)=24$ under the new
drug and $Y(0)=20$ under standard care. (a) State her individual treatment effect $\tau(\omega)$. (b) If
Alice is assigned the new drug, write down her observed outcome $Y$ and her counterfactual (hidden)
outcome, and do the same if she is assigned standard care. (c) In one sentence, explain why, no matter
which treatment she receives, we can never compute her ITE from her data alone, citing
@thm-fundamental-problem.
:::

::: {#exr-po-interpret-estimand}
## Interpretation: which estimand answers the question?
**(Interpretation.)** For each question below, name which of the ATE, ATT, ATC, or CATE it asks for, and
say (one clause) which population the average is over. (a) "Across all eligible patients, how much would
average function improve if everyone switched from standard care to the new drug?" (b) "Among the patients
who actually received the new drug, how much did it help on average?" (c) "For favorable-baseline patients
specifically, what is the average benefit?" (d) A regulator asks what the drug did for the people who took
it. Which estimand, and why does the answer differ from (a) when treatment was not randomized?
:::

::: {#exr-po-recompute}
## Recomputing the worked example
**(Computation.)** Repeat @exm-confounding-gformula with the propensities changed to $e(0)=0.1$ and
$e(1)=0.9$, keeping the covariate law and all four conditional means $\mu_t(x)$ unchanged. (a) Recompute
the within-arm covariate distributions $P(X=1\mid T=1)$ and $P(X=1\mid T=0)$. (b) Recompute the naive
contrast $\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}$. (c) Verify the selection-bias decomposition @eq-naive-decomposition
numerically, and confirm that the standardized contrast @eq-ate-identification still equals $4$. (d)
Explain in one sentence why sharper confounding (more extreme propensities) enlarges the bias while leaving
the ATE untouched.
:::

::: {#exr-po-masked-identity}
## The masked-outcome identities
**(Computation and proof.)** Using only $T\in\{0,1\}$ and the consistency identity @eq-consistency-identity,
prove the two masked identities @eq-consistency-masked, $TY=TY(1)$ and $(1-T)Y=(1-T)Y(0)$, and deduce that
$\mathbb{E}[TY]=\mathbb{E}[TY(1)]$ and $\mathbb{E}[(1-T)Y]=\mathbb{E}[(1-T)Y(0)]$ for any population. Explain
why these identities require no ignorability assumption.
:::

::: {#exr-po-att-atc}
## ATE, ATT, and ATC in the worked example
**(Computation.)** In the population of @exm-confounding-gformula, compute the ATT $\tau_{\mathrm{T}}$ and
the ATC $\tau_{\mathrm{C}}$ directly from their definitions, and verify the decomposition
$\tau=p\,\tau_{\mathrm{T}}+(1-p)\,\tau_{\mathrm{C}}$ of @prp-ate-att-atc with $p=P(T=1)$. Then modify a
single conditional mean so that the CATE is no longer constant, and show that ATT and ATC now differ while
the decomposition still holds.
:::

::: {#exr-po-mean-vs-weak}
## Mean ignorability is strictly weaker
**(Proof.)** Construct a joint law for $(Y(1),T,X)$ in which mean ignorability
$\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid X]$ holds but weak ignorability $Y(1)\perp T\mid X$ fails.
(Hint: use the two-row template of @sec-po-assumptions; fix a single stratum $X=x$ and give $Y(1)$ the same
conditional mean but different conditional variances across $T=0$ and $T=1$, for instance the values
$\{9,11\}$ among the treated and $\{5,15\}$ among the untreated.) Prove carefully that the conditional means
are equal (so mean ignorability holds) yet the conditional laws differ (so weak ignorability fails). Confirm
that the identification of $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$ in @lem-mean-potential-identification still goes through,
illustrating that the proof uses only the first moment.
:::

::: {#exr-po-positivity-failure}
## Positivity failure breaks identification ($\star$)
**(Proof.)** Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=1)=\tfrac12$, and suppose treatment is deterministic in one
stratum: $e(0)=P(T=1\mid X=0)=0$ while $e(1)=0.5$. Keep SUTVA and strong ignorability. As a preliminary,
draw the $2\times 2$ table of the four cells $\{X=x,T=t\}$ and mark which cell is *empty* (has probability
zero); this empty cell is the whole source of the failure. Then: (a) Show that $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1,X=0]$
is undefined, so the right-hand side of the adjustment formula @eq-ate-identification cannot be evaluated.
(b) Exhibit two values of $\mu_1(0)=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid X=0]$, consistent with the same observed-data law,
that yield different ATEs, thereby proving the ATE is not identified when positivity fails. (c) Relate this
to the covariate-overlap requirement for indirect comparisons discussed in @sec-po-bridge.
*(Solution in Appendix F.)*
:::

::: {#exr-po-selection-bias-proof}
## A symmetric selection-bias decomposition ($\star$)
**(Challenge.)** Prove the control-side analogue of @thm-naive-selection-bias:
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tau_{\mathrm{C}}+\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=0]\bigr),
$$
by adding and subtracting $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid T=0]$ instead of $\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid T=1]$ in the proof.
Then average the two decompositions (the ATT-side of @eq-naive-decomposition and this ATC-side) to express
$\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}$ as a half-and-half combination, and interpret the resulting symmetric bias term.
Show that under marginal ignorability both bias terms vanish, recovering @cor-naive-unbiased-rct.
*(Solution in Appendix F.)*
:::
